stories.headline: Pirro Drops All Remaining Reflecting Pool Charges After Evidence Shows Construction Flaw, Despite Trump Rebuke
stories.summary:
Federal prosecutors in Washington, D.C., dismissed criminal charges against the three remaining defendants accused of vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, completing a full collapse of the case days after U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office dropped a felony charge against former Olympic canoeist David Hearn. Court filings show the cases against Justin Carreno, Sophie Dennison-Gibby, and Cameron Thiers — each facing misdemeanor charges of destroying property valued under $1,000 — are now marked closed.

The dismissals follow Interior Department evidence, obtained after Hearn's indictment, showing the pool damage resulted from a "rushed and flawed installation" of the pool lining rather than vandalism. Prosecutors stated that Interior officials withheld this critical evidence until after a grand jury had already indicted Hearn, a complication that forced the case's collapse.

President Trump publicly rebuked Pirro before the additional dismissals, saying she "choked" and "folded like an umbrella," and writing on Truth Social that he disagreed "100%" with her decision. Pirro subsequently brought a large box of Interior Department evidence to a reportedly heated private Oval Office meeting with Trump, where she presented the exculpatory material directly to the president.

The episode has highlighted a rare public rift between Trump and one of his own U.S. attorneys. Supporters of the prosecution argue vandalism did occur at the renovated landmark, while critics of the charges — and now prosecutors themselves — say the evidence points to contractor failures, not criminal conduct. The White House referred questions about the additional dismissals to Trump's earlier Oval Office remarks.

stories.headline: Update: Abdul El-Sayed Leads Haley Stevens in Too-Close Michigan Senate Democratic Primary
stories.summary:
The Michigan Democratic Senate primary between progressive physician Abdul El-Sayed and four-term Rep. Haley Stevens remained unresolved Wednesday morning, with El-Sayed holding a razor-thin 48.5% to 47.5% lead — far narrower than polls had projected. Most surveys had El-Sayed ahead by double digits, including an Emerson poll showing a 16-point margin. El-Sayed declared victory and NBC News called the race for him, though the Associated Press had not yet confirmed a winner as of midday.

The race has served as a bellwether for the direction of the Democratic Party. El-Sayed, backed by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders, campaigned on opposition to large-money super PACs and U.S. military aid to Israel, calling Israel's Gaza operation a genocide. Stevens, supported by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, and the pro-Israel group AIPAC — which spent more than $30 million on her behalf — represented the party's establishment wing.

The surprisingly close margin suggests AIPAC's investment and establishment backing had more traction than polls indicated, even as a third candidate, suspended campaigner Mallory McMorrow, captured roughly 4% of the vote. El-Sayed has faced criticism that his positions on Israel alienate Jewish voters, a charge he has pushed back on by arguing he is trying to build a broad coalition around bread-and-butter issues like housing and healthcare.

The outcome carries national implications for the Democratic Party's identity heading into the 2026 midterms, with progressive forces testing their strength against incumbents and establishment figures in multiple states. Leaked audio also surfaced of El-Sayed signaling interest in future primary challenges, adding to the friction within the party.

stories.headline: RFK Jr. Decertifies Kentucky Organ Procurement Organization Over Coerced Harvesting Findings
stories.summary:
Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced Wednesday that the federal government has decertified Network for Hope, the nonprofit organ procurement organization serving Kentucky and parts of Ohio, West Virginia, and Indiana, following a yearlong investigation. Federal reviewers found "persistent patient safety failures" including pursuing organ retrieval without confirming donor death, despite repeated warnings and corrective action plans.

The action stems in part from the case of Anthony Thomas "TJ" Hoover II, a Kentucky man who nearly died of a drug overdose in 2021 and was being prepared for organ retrieval surgery while still conscious — reportedly "thrashing, crying, and grabbing the doctor's hands to stop him," according to his sister Donna Rohrer, who spoke at Wednesday's press conference. A federal investigation found the organization similarly ignored signs of alertness in more than 70 other patients, with over 100 additional cases showing "concerning features."

The decertification follows a congressional investigation led by House Energy and Commerce Committee Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-KY) and mirrors a September 2025 action in which HHS decertified a University of Miami Health System organ procurement organization for unsafe practices. Whistleblowers from New Jersey also came forward in November to describe similar conduct at other organizations.

The case has renewed scrutiny of the national organ procurement system, which critics argue operates with insufficient oversight. Advocates for organ donation note that registered donor numbers have already declined in recent years amid public concern over transplant coordinators' conduct, and further erosion of public trust could affect the availability of organs for patients in need.

stories.headline: AP Investigation: Over 50 Military Spouses and Parents Detained Under Trump Immigration Crackdown
stories.summary:
An Associated Press investigation has found that more than 50 parents and spouses of active-duty U.S. military personnel have been detained since President Trump began his second term, with at least six deported, one self-deported, and eight still in federal immigration custody. The AP compiled the figures by analyzing thousands of federal court records, as the Department of Homeland Security does not track such cases, and noted the actual number is likely higher.

For decades, bipartisan consensus has shielded military family members from deportation as a matter of national security and morale. The reversal has delayed deployments, forced service members to take leave, and left some without caretakers for their children. "How can I even focus on my military career because I have to worry about how my wife is doing?" said Army Sgt. Hedar Leonel Turcios Juarez, whose wife was detained outside a Texas Walmart in front of their 6-year-old daughter.

DHS has defended the detentions, noting that some individuals had prior removal orders, had been previously deported, or had criminal records including DUI and drug-related convictions. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has intervened in a handful of high-profile cases to secure releases following public backlash. The military continues to recruit by advertising immigration benefits for enlistees' families even as those protections are being curtailed.

Experts warn the policy shift could undermine military readiness, particularly as the U.S. remains engaged in conflict with Iran. Supporters of strict enforcement argue immigration law must apply uniformly regardless of family connections, while critics — including military families and legal advocates — contend the policy breaks a long-standing compact with service members and damages force cohesion.

stories.headline: DOJ Charges 19 in Medicaid Fraud Sweep as Strike Force Tops $45 Billion Nationally
stories.summary:
The Justice Department on Tuesday charged 19 defendants in Philadelphia-area schemes that generated more than $4 million in fraudulent Medicare and Medicaid claims, simultaneously expanding its Northeast Health Care Fraud Strike Force into the city. Defendants include home health aides, Medicaid recipients, and owners and employees of home care companies. Alleged schemes include billing for services never rendered — in some cases while aides were incarcerated, hospitalized, or traveling overseas — and one aide who reportedly claimed to provide care to seven recipients simultaneously, submitting claims for more than 24 hours of work in a single day.

The announcements were made alongside a new partnership between the DOJ's National Fraud Enforcement Division and the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz highlighted Pennsylvania as a state warranting heightened scrutiny, noting it ranks fifth nationally in average monthly Medicaid payments per beneficiary and that more than 96% of personal-care claims are coded with the vague designation 'illness unspecified,' complicating fraud detection.

Nationally, the Health Care Fraud Strike Force has now prosecuted more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal programs and private insurers more than $45 billion. The milestone figure underscores the scale of the administration's anti-fraud effort across the healthcare sector.

Supporters of the crackdown argue it protects taxpayers and ensures resources reach genuinely vulnerable patients. Critics of broader Medicaid enforcement have previously warned that aggressive fraud investigations can create compliance burdens for legitimate home care providers, particularly in communities with limited administrative capacity — though no such objections were raised in response to Tuesday's specific charges.

stories.headline: Mountaineering World Mourns Loss of Nirmal Purja and Five Elite Nepali Guides in Broad Peak Avalanche
stories.summary:
Six Nepali mountaineers, including celebrated British-Nepali climber Nirmal 'Nims' Purja, were killed last week in an avalanche on Pakistan's Broad Peak, the world's 12th-highest mountain. Purja, 43, was internationally renowned for summiting all 14 peaks above 8,000 meters in just over six months, a record widely considered one of the greatest achievements in modern mountaineering history. He was leading a 10-member international expedition when the avalanche struck.

Among the others killed were Kili Pemba Sherpa, who had just completed his own ascent of all 14 eight-thousanders in early July and was part of the historic first winter ascent of K2 in 2021, and Pur Bahadur Gurung, one of only 100 Nepali guides certified by the International Federation of Mountain Guides Association. Fellow guides and mountaineering experts described the deaths as a catastrophic and irreplaceable loss for Nepal's climbing community.

The six climbers collectively represented decades of achievement that had fundamentally elevated the global recognition of Nepali guides — historically regarded as support staff — to elite athletes and expedition leaders in their own right. Nepal's tourism department called it 'unprecedented loss.'

The deaths come amid a broader reckoning in the mountaineering world over safety conditions on the world's highest peaks, where commercial expedition traffic has increased significantly in recent years. Authorities and the climbing community are expected to examine conditions on Broad Peak in the aftermath of the disaster.

stories.headline: AI Displacement Hollows Out Philippines' $40 Billion Outsourcing Industry
stories.summary:
Workers in the Philippines' business process outsourcing sector — an industry employing roughly 1.9 million people and accounting for approximately 10% of the country's GDP — are losing jobs at an accelerating pace as companies replace content writers, customer service agents, and other white-collar roles with generative AI. Multiple former employees described to the BBC a pattern in which they were first asked to edit AI-generated material, then used to train AI systems on company style, before being made redundant. 'I feel like I dug my own grave,' said one former content writer who was let go one month before her position was due to become permanent.

The Philippines is disproportionately exposed to this shift. The International Labour Organization estimates that 12.7 million Filipinos — more than one in four workers — are employed in occupations exposed to generative AI, the highest share in Southeast Asia. The outsourcing sector, built over two decades with government investment and tax incentives for multinationals including Accenture, Concentrix, and Teleperformance, was designed precisely around the kinds of routine cognitive tasks that AI now performs cheaply and rapidly.

The human stakes are significant: the BPO sector lifted large portions of the Philippine middle class and serves as the country's second-largest source of foreign exchange after overseas remittances. Economists warn that unlike previous technological transitions, AI displacement in this sector may be rapid and offer fewer adjacent jobs for displaced workers to move into.

The Philippine situation is being watched as a leading indicator for other emerging economies whose development models relied on English-language service exports. Policymakers face pressure to reskill workers and attract higher-value investment, but there is as yet no clear national strategy for managing the transition at scale.

stories.headline: South Korean Police Raid Starbucks Korea Headquarters Over 'Tank Day' Marketing Controversy
stories.summary:
South Korean police raided the national headquarters of Starbucks Korea on Wednesday as part of a criminal investigation into defamation claims stemming from a May marketing campaign. The promotion, dubbed 'Tank Day,' was launched on the anniversary of the 1980 Gwangju Uprising — in which hundreds of pro-democracy protesters were killed by military forces under dictator Chun Doo-hwan — and featured a coffee tumbler whose name many Koreans interpreted as a reference to the tanks used to crush the uprising. Starbucks withdrew the campaign and said the connection was unintentional, but civic groups filed a criminal complaint alleging the company defamed victims.

The fallout was severe. Starbucks Korea, operated by the Shinsegae Group, fired its chief executive, temporarily closed stores nationwide for mandatory staff history lessons, and reported a serious decline in sales in one of the chain's largest global markets. A police raid on company headquarters marks a significant escalation of the legal consequences from what began as a marketing error.

The episode became deeply politicized. President Lee Jae-myung condemned the campaign as an insult to the victims of Gwangju, and his government announced a boycott of Starbucks outlets. The main opposition party pushed back, with its leader holding up a Starbucks cup during a speech and accusing the government of overreach. Starbucks cups subsequently became a symbol adopted by right-wing commentators opposing the Lee administration.

The promotional material compounded the offense with a secondary historical reference: it used the phrase 'tak on the table,' mimicking a sound associated with a controversial 1987 police statement about the death of a student activist in custody. The dual resonance amplified public outrage and turned a product launch into a national controversy touching on South Korea's most sensitive modern history.

stories.headline: Cyclospora Outbreak Surpasses 20,000 Suspected Cases Across Nearly All U.S. States
stories.summary:
A cyclospora outbreak linked to contaminated lettuce has now produced more than 20,000 suspected cases in the United States, with all but three states reporting infections, according to CBS News. New cases have been confirmed in Missouri and Arkansas, expanding the geographic footprint of what has become one of the largest foodborne illness outbreaks in recent memory.

Cyclosporiasis is caused by the parasite Cyclospora cayetanensis and typically causes prolonged, watery diarrhea, fatigue, and stomach cramps. The illness can last weeks if untreated. Public health officials have linked the outbreak to lettuce, though a specific supplier or distribution chain has not been publicly identified in available reporting.

The scale of the outbreak — spanning nearly the entire country and exceeding 20,000 suspected cases — places it firmly in the category of a major public health event. Federal health authorities have not yet issued a formal national recall of implicated lettuce products based on reporting available today, but the rapid spread across additional states signals the outbreak has not been contained.

stories.headline: UN Rights Chief Sounds Alarm Over Surge in Iranian Executions Since March
stories.summary:
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk issued a formal statement Wednesday expressing alarm at a sharp increase in executions in Iran, saying capital punishment is being used to "instil fear among the population and suppress dissent." He said at least 56 people have been executed on national security-related charges since March 19, including 27 connected to January's nationwide anti-government protests, with more than 100 others at risk of execution on similar charges.

Iran executed at least 2,159 people in 2025 according to Amnesty International, the highest figure recorded since 1981 and including 45 executions of suspected dissidents. More recent cases include the execution of 19-year-old Arvin Kheirkhahan, convicted of "enmity against God" for alleged participation in January's unrest, and two men convicted of spying for Israel's Mossad. Türk said several executions followed a single three-hour closed-door hearing and that confessions were allegedly obtained under torture.

The Iranian government has not responded directly to Türk's statement but has previously defended its use of the death penalty, saying it is reserved for "the most severe crimes." Activists have warned that the combination of January's protests, during which thousands were killed and tens of thousands detained, and the February war with the United States and Israel has accelerated the use of executions as a tool of political repression.

Türk called on Iranian authorities to halt all executions and move toward abolition of the death penalty. The statement adds international pressure on Tehran at a moment when it is already isolated following the recent conflict and ongoing nuclear tensions.

stories.headline: Colombia Becomes First Latin American Country to Ban Female Genital Mutilation
stories.summary:
Colombia's Congress passed legislation last week unanimously banning female genital mutilation, making it the first country in Latin America to criminalize the practice. The law follows years of activism, including by members of the Emberá Indigenous community where FGM has been practiced in secret, often performed on infants and girls under six years old. Between 2020 and June 2026, 240 cases were recorded in Colombia, though medical professionals say that figure represents only a fraction of actual occurrences.

Activists and medical workers say girls and women subjected to FGM face serious health consequences including hemorrhage, infection, complications during childbirth, and lifelong pain. The World Health Organization estimates more than 230 million girls and women alive today have undergone the procedure globally, predominantly in Africa. In Colombia, the practice has been concentrated within specific Indigenous communities, and some girls believed to have died from a traditional illness called "jai" are now thought by advocates to have died from FGM complications.

The unanimous congressional vote is described by advocates as a milestone both for Colombia and for the broader Latin American region, which had no country-level ban on the practice prior to this legislation. The law also opens a debate about how governments balance criminal enforcement with the cultural and community dimensions of the practice, particularly in Indigenous communities where it has been carried out for generations.

stories.headline: Update: Russia Kills 21 in Deadliest Strike on Kyiv This Year; Zelensky Warns of Interceptor Shortage
stories.summary:
Russia launched a massive overnight attack on Ukraine using 24 ballistic missiles, four anti-ship missiles, and 115 drones, killing at least 21 people across Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Donetsk. Kyiv and its surrounding region suffered the deadliest strikes of the year, with residential buildings, a railway station, and warehouses hit. Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 98 of the 115 drones but failed to stop any of the ballistic missiles.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the deaths were preventable, stating that more U.S.-made Patriot missile interceptors 'could have saved lives' and that the supply of anti-ballistic systems from allies had been 'significantly reduced' this year. BBC Verify analysis of Ukrainian air force data shows missile interceptions have dropped 22% compared to the same period last year, while Russia has increased its missile launches by 83% over the same window.

Russia's defense ministry said it targeted logistics hubs and supply centers involved in storing and delivering weapons, as well as three cargo vessels near Odesa allegedly carrying military equipment. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko warned that people may be trapped under rubble. Fires were still burning across approximately 230,000 square meters of the Kyiv region as of Wednesday morning.

The attack marks a significant escalation in Russia's aerial campaign against Ukrainian cities. The strike renews pressure on Western governments — particularly the United States — to accelerate delivery of air defense interceptors, a request Kyiv has made repeatedly throughout the conflict.

stories.headline: House Democrats Add 12 Republican-Held Districts to Midterm Target List With 90 Days to Election
stories.summary:
The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee announced Wednesday it is expanding its offensive map by adding 12 Republican-held or Republican-leaning congressional districts to its 2026 midterm target list, including seats held by Rep. Lauren Boebert of Colorado and Rep. Richard Hudson of North Carolina — the chair of the Republican counterpart, the NRCC. The move comes exactly 90 days before the November midterm elections.

The additions are intended to signal Democratic confidence that the party can compete in territory President Trump carried comfortably in 2024. Republicans have dismissed the expanded map as an exercise in projection, arguing that Democrats lack the resources and candidate quality to seriously contest seats in reliably red districts. The DCCC's announcement also coincided with Rep. Chuck Edwards of North Carolina dropping his re-election bid after the House Ethics Committee recommended his censure following a finding that he fostered a hostile work environment and engaged in sexual harassment of two young female staffers.

Edwards, who denied wrongdoing, said he would complete his current term but not seek re-election — a development that adds another competitive opening to the Democratic map. His district in Western North Carolina now becomes a potential target.

With control of the House at stake, both parties are intensifying their resource allocation in the final stretch. Democrats need a net gain of seats to reclaim the majority, and the DCCC's expansion of the battlefield reflects a broader Democratic argument that the political environment has shifted in their favor since 2024.

stories.headline: Federal Appeals Court Blocks EPA From Terminating $20 Billion in Biden-Era Clean Energy Grants
stories.summary:
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit ruled Tuesday that the Environmental Protection Agency cannot suspend or terminate $20 billion in clean energy grants issued under the Biden administration's Inflation Reduction Act. The decision reinstates a preliminary injunction originally issued by District Judge Tanya Chutkan in April 2025, which had barred the EPA from 'unlawfully suspending or terminating' the grants.

The funds at issue were distributed from the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund to eight nonprofit organizations for clean energy projects nationwide. The EPA under Administrator Lee Zeldin had frozen and sought to terminate the grants, arguing that the Biden administration improperly routed the money through Citibank in a rushed disbursement before leaving office. Zeldin has referred to the funds as 'gold bars,' citing a video in which a former EPA employee described an urgent push to spend down the money before the end of the administration.

Six of the court's ten panel judges agreed that the EPA likely violated the law when it sought to terminate grants and claw back funds that had already been disbursed, ruling the agency acted 'based solely on a policy disagreement.' Climate United, one of the three grantees that brought the litigation, said the ruling confirmed there was 'no legal basis' for the EPA's actions. The EPA can still appeal to the Supreme Court.

The ruling is a significant legal setback for the Trump administration's efforts to unwind Biden-era climate spending and is likely to intensify the broader legal battle over the Inflation Reduction Act's implementation. Supporters of the grants argue the funds are already deployed in communities; critics contend the disbursement process was designed to circumvent incoming administration oversight.

stories.headline: Pakistan Imposes New Restrictions on International Media, Requiring Permits to Report Outside Three Cities
stories.summary:
Pakistani authorities have introduced sweeping new regulations requiring all foreign media organizations — including Pakistani nationals working for international outlets — to obtain government permission before reporting from anywhere in the country outside the cities of Islamabad, Karachi, and Lahore. The rules, issued Sunday and called the Foreign Media Facilitation Guidelines 2026, immediately drew condemnation from press freedom organizations and senior journalists.

The guidelines do not specify how long the permitting process, known as a No Objection Certificate, may take — a significant concern given that foreign journalists already face waits of months or indefinite delays under existing NOC requirements. The new rules effectively extend that permitting regime to Pakistani freelancers and contributors based outside the three designated cities, who have historically served as the primary means for international outlets to cover breaking news in areas like Peshawar and Quetta.

The government defended the guidelines as an administrative mechanism to verify credentials and coordinate media access, not as a restriction on reporting. However, Zaffar Abbas, editor of the Dawn newspaper, called the restrictions 'totally unacceptable,' saying he had never seen their like in 40 years of journalism through multiple military and civilian governments. The guidelines also allow authorities to revoke journalist accreditation for conduct deemed to affect 'ideology, sovereignty, security or public order' — terms critics described as dangerously vague.

Pakistan currently ranks 153rd out of 180 countries on the World Press Freedom Index. The restrictions come as the country faces ongoing political instability, with elections in Kashmir proceeding under an internet blackout. Journalist organizations warn the new rules will severely curtail independent reporting on security situations, natural disasters, and political unrest across much of the country's territory.

stories.headline: Armed Man with Illegal Weapons Arrested Near Trump Golf Course Ahead of Presidential Visit
stories.summary:
Authorities arrested Jeanine John Taele, 38, on Sunday at Trump National Golf Course in Rancho Palos Verdes, California, where President Trump was scheduled to attend a Republican fundraising dinner on Tuesday. Plainclothes federal agents initially spotted Taele walking the grounds and photographing security arrangements, then alerted local sheriff's deputies. He was found carrying a 16-round magazine with hollow-point ammunition and was separately wanted in connection with a robbery in El Segundo.

A subsequent search of Taele's vehicle uncovered a loaded pistol and additional illegal ammunition. FBI Joint Terrorism Task Force agents and the LA County Sheriff's Major Crimes Bureau raided his Downey residence on Monday, finding an illegally modified AR-platform rifle, a .45 caliber pistol, body armor, high-capacity magazines, large quantities of ammunition, and multiple notebooks described as containing 'concerning statements.'

Taele faces charges of carrying a concealed firearm and possession of armor-piercing prohibited ammunition, with authorities indicating additional charges may follow. The Los Angeles Sheriff's Department said no 'credible threat to our communities' has been identified but called the case a demonstration of the importance of law enforcement vigilance. The US Secret Service is assisting with the ongoing investigation.

The arrest occurred during a rare presidential trip to California, where Trump was also scheduled to deliver remarks critical of Governor Gavin Newsom. The incident is the latest in a series of security scares surrounding the president and underscores persistent concerns about threats against senior officials.

stories.headline: Update: Spokane Arson Suspect Linked to Two Prior Fire Investigations as Wildfires Continue to Burn
stories.summary:
Aaron Farinacci, 37, the man arrested on suspicion of deliberately igniting the largest of three wildfires burning around Spokane, Washington, was previously linked to two separate arson investigations last summer, though he was never charged in those cases, the Spokane County Sheriff said Tuesday. Farinacci appeared in court via video link but did not enter a plea. He is being held on a $1 million bond on a first-degree arson charge.

Farinacci was spotted kneeling near grass at the fire's origin point and was found carrying matches and a lighter when stopped by authorities. Investigators eliminated other ignition sources, including train activity and electrical infrastructure, before concluding the blaze was likely started by matches or a lighter. Court records also reveal a 2010 manslaughter conviction for the killing of his father.

The three Spokane fires — Old Trails, Fairview, and Autumn Lane — have destroyed more than 700 structures and forced over 60,000 residents to evacuate. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson called the situation a 'nightmare' and likely the worst natural disaster in Spokane's history. No deaths or injuries have been confirmed, though authorities said they had been unable to reach 14 individuals by phone.

Firefighters made some progress against two of the blazes on Tuesday amid lighter winds and cooler temperatures, but officials warned conditions could worsen later in the week. The fires are among 16 burning across Washington state.

stories.headline: Update: Idaho In-N-Out Gunman Identified; Armed Bystander Credited with Limiting Casualties
stories.summary:
Police have identified the gunman who killed three people and wounded seven others at an In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, on Saturday as Chad Williams, 24. Williams fatally shot himself following the attack. Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks confirmed Williams acted alone; a motive has not been established. Two of the seven wounded remained in critical condition as of Sunday.

An armed bystander and an off-duty state police officer who happened to be present both returned fire at Williams, actions the police chief called heroic and credited with driving the gunman away and likely preventing further casualties. In-N-Out Burger President Lynsi Snyder confirmed one of those killed was a company employee and expressed grief over the attack.

The shooting prompted a shelter-in-place order across a busy commercial corridor that includes a mall and movie theater complex, affecting hundreds of potential witnesses. The order was subsequently lifted. The Twin Falls In-N-Out location had opened just days before the attack, on July 24.

Authorities said hundreds of witnesses are expected to be interviewed as the investigation into Williams's motive continues. The incident has renewed attention to questions about mass shootings at public commercial locations and to the role of armed civilians in such emergencies.

stories.headline: Bangladesh's Exiled Former Premier Hasina Vows Return Despite Death Sentence
stories.summary:
Former Bangladeshi Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who has been living in exile in India since being ousted in a mass uprising in August 2024, declared Tuesday that she intends to return to Bangladesh despite facing a death sentence issued by courts in the country following her removal from power. Hasina described the return as her 'duty,' warning that Bangladesh was sliding into economic distress and democratic decline under its current leadership.

Hasina, who led Bangladesh for 15 consecutive years, was forced to flee as protests against her government turned deadly. Her return would represent an extraordinary political gamble given the capital charges she faces and the hostile political environment that accompanied her ouster. Bangladesh's interim government, led by Nobel laureate Muhammad Yunus, has overseen prosecutions of Hasina and senior figures from her Awami League party.

The announcement introduces fresh uncertainty into Bangladesh's already volatile political transition. Hasina's supporters see her as a stabilizing figure capable of restoring order; her opponents argue her return would inflame tensions and undermine accountability for abuses alleged during her tenure.

Bangladesh's political future remains contested, with elections expected but no firm date set. Hasina's declaration is likely to energize both her supporters and her adversaries and could complicate diplomatic relations between India, where she has been sheltering, and Dhaka.
